extracted.intended_audience: inventors and patent practitioners (patent attorneys, agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal rules for preparing a patent specification (disclosure) — what to describe, how much detail, what may/may not be omitted or relied on, for machines, manufactures, methods and chemical products. Focused on common-law case guidance for sufficiency and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings may substitute for scale when enabling
rubrics_metrics.description: If a common mechanic can make the subject of the patent from the drawing in perspective, it is not necessary that there should be a scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically a scale was required (Arkwright), but modernly a perspective drawing that enables a skilled workman suffices. Example: Arkwright's machine could not be made for want of a scale; later authorities allow drawings to be 'called in aid' of the specification if, by comparison of words and drawings, a skilful mechanic can perform the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings can be as good as written description when enabling
rubrics_metrics.description: A drawing or figure which enables a workman of ordinary skill to construct the improvement is as good as any written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While earlier rules said the specification should be sufficiently descriptive in words and not rely on diagrams alone, courts have held that drawings enabling manufacture satisfy the disclosure requirement (Bloxam v. Elsee and subsequent authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must be in apt words intelligible to mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification ought to be made in apt words, intelligible to mechanics; a person is not bound to look at the diagram to learn the invention, unless the words and drawings together explain the invention sufficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-English terms or odd names may be immaterial if the drawing and relative proportions allow a mechanic to construct the machine; but reliance on drawings to cure wholly unintelligible wording is risky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means must be adapted to the end (no irrelevant or misleading alternatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: The means must be adapted to the end; the description must not give several ways and methods which may or may not answer, according to the skill exercised in the attempt to produce the manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: listing many salts when only one actually produces the effect (Winter) renders the specification void. Avoid enumerating alternatives that mislead the public into thinking multiple options work when only one does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not describe effects that cannot be produced
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects that cannot accurately be produced must not be mentioned and described; the patentee should inform the inquirer of the exact nature of the manufacture invented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the article lacks the qualities, or the machine does not produce the results set forth, the grant is invalid. Courts will set aside patents where claimed results are not realizable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility with local materials or methods must be shown
rubrics_metrics.description: If a material or process used by the inventor (e.g., a specially prepared charcoal) cannot be shown to be usable in the jurisdiction, the patentee must prove either that local equivalents will work, that extraction or preparation is simple and known, or otherwise show reproducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derosne v. Fairie: inventor used charcoal made abroad with doubtful properties; failure to disclose how to obtain or make equivalent material locally led to a new trial / invalidation risk. Explain how to obtain or prepare specialized inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must disclose the exact nature and properties of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must inform the public of the exact nature of the manufacture invented; omissions about qualities or results that are claimed will invalidate the grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not claim broader qualities or results than can actually be produced; be accurate about capabilities and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: If patent claims multiple things, claim only what is truly invented
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must not claim more than his invention; if a patent is taken for several things and he fails in any one of them (or claims more than his invention), the specification may be incorrect or the patent void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases differ: if one claimed item is not new the grant can fail in toto; if one claimed item later proves useless, earlier cases suggest the grant may still be valid. Courts scrutinize whether the specification claims the whole machine when only an improvement was invented (Browne/lace engine, Browne v. Wigley analogues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish new parts from old (do not monopolize pre-existing subject-matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patent is for an improvement or addition, the inventor cannot monopolize the whole subject; the specification is incorrect if it contains description of more than the improvement unless it particularly distinguishes the new from the old parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention is a new combination added to existing combinations, describe only the new combinations and how they are added. If prior combinations existed, claim only the additional combinations that are truly new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full and fair disclosure of all known to the patentee (best mode)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must give the subject to the public in the best and most improved state known to the inventor at the time; if the inventor knew of a more beneficial mode and omitted it, the patent is void as fraudulent concealment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: rubbing tempered steel with tallow; use of aqua fortis in making verdigris; bending teeth in a lace machine. Even insignificant-known improvements must be disclosed. If the better mode was discovered after the grant, the patent may remain valid but a presumption of concealment arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadvertent omission of a known better mode can void the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inventor actually knew and meant to practise a better mode and inadvertently did not state it in the specification, he must answer for his inadvertence and the patent may be void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat inadvertence seriously; the jury may be asked whether concealment or inadvertence occurred (Boville v. Moore examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between disclosed materials and actual practice
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee uses cheaper or different materials in practice than those enumerated, his grant will not be sustained simply by proving that the enumerated materials would answer the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mislead by listing only expensive or unusual ingredients that the patentee does not actually require; disclose what will enable the public to practice the invention with the same advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of detail for machines: minute but not overwrought; enable a reasonable-skilled mechanic
rubrics_metrics.description: The description of a machine must disclose the nature of the invention and the manner in which it is to be performed. It must be minute without perplexity, and luminous without being overwrought. It should be such that a common mechanic, with a reasonable degree of skill, may comprehend it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not describe elementary or universally known elements at unnecessary length, but do not omit necessary particulars. No inventive faculty should be exercised by the reader; avoid leaving essential matters to trial or experiment unless data/manner/results are so clear that it may easily be done. The jury decides what constitutes reasonable skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify parts, proportions, unions and relative motions for machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing machinery, set forth several parts (wheels, rollers, screws, springs, etc.), their proportions (diameters, thickness, tension), the method by which they are united, and the relative velocities of the movable parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parts are to be attached/removed during operation or used for multiple purposes, state what they are, proportions for different purposes, and where to apply them. If components of two machines are combined, clearly show the union of the parts that make up each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to scientific rudiments permitted but not to substitute for disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference may be made to the rudiments of the science by which the principles of the machine are explained, but not to scientific books as a substitute for the inventor's disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propositions or truths generally known need no reference; material only found in particular treatises must be explained rather than merely cited, and must not be claimed as new without explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method or principle patents must be described with exceptional accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: If a method is the subject-matter of the patent (i.e., tangible means carrying the method into practice are claimed), the description must be so clear and evident that no experiments are necessary to learn it and to put it in practice as beneficially as the patentee enjoys it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because principles or pure methods are problematic as patent subjects, the specification of any method is governed by the same rigorous rules as for machines/manufactures: enablement without need for inventive trial, full particulars of the tangible means, and clarity of operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical inventions: disclose ingredients, proportions, process timing and uses
rubrics_metrics.description: When a chemical discovery is the foundation of the invention, the substance produced (not the abstract principle) ought to be described; the ingredients, their proportions, the time of mixing, etc., ought to be fully stated, and the beneficial use to which the substance can be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must enable the public to make the chemical with the same advantages and with as little expense and labor as the inventor; concealment of a valuable reagent or step (e.g., aqua fortis) is prejudicial and voids the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining previously patented or known subjects: describe method of combination
rubrics_metrics.description: If the combination consists of the subjects of several patents which have expired, or of some new ones bought, a description of the method by which they were combined, with a reference to the several specifications, may be sufficient to sustain the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the new invention is merely a particular way of combining known parts, the specification should show how they are combined and where the novelty lies (Ellenborough CJ reasoning).
